primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Hell' primarily signifies the final state or place of divine punishment and separation from God for the unrepentant wicked after death and final judgment. It is symbolically depicted through images of unquenchable fire, darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth, and destruction (drawing on the Greek term Gehenna, itself derived from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a site associated with idolatrous burning and later with fiery judgment). The dominant traditional reading takes this as eternal conscious punishment and exclusion from God's presence.
primary_basis: Matthew 25:41, 46 (eternal fire prepared for the devil; eternal punishment vs. eternal life)
Mark 9:43-48 (Gehenna, where 'their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched')
Matthew 10:28 (fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna)
Matthew 5:22, 29-30 (danger of the fire of Gehenna)
Matthew 13:41-42, 49-50 (fiery furnace, weeping and gnashing of teeth)
Luke 16:19-31 (the rich man in torment in Hades)
2 Thessalonians 1:9 (eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord)
Revelation 14:9-11 (smoke of their torment rises forever)
Jude 7 (Sodom as an example, undergoing punishment of eternal fire)

alternatives.meaning: Eternal conscious torment (traditionalist view): Hell is unending, conscious punishment of the wicked, whether the fire is literal or metaphorical for real anguish. This is the historic majority position of Catholic, Orthodox, and most Protestant confessions (e.g., Augustine, Aquinas, Westminster Confession).

Metaphorical/relational view: the fire, darkness, and worm imagery are symbols not to be taken literally; hell's essence is self-chosen exclusion and separation from God (a view articulated by figures such as C.S. Lewis and reflected in the Catechism of the Catholic Church's language of 'definitive self-exclusion from communion with God').

Annihilationism / conditional immortality: the wicked are ultimately destroyed and cease to exist rather than suffering forever; 'eternal punishment' means punishment with eternal (irreversible) results. Advocated by John Stott, Edward Fudge, Seventh-day Adventists, and a growing evangelical minority.

Universal reconciliation (universalism): hell is real but remedial/purgative and temporary, with all persons ultimately reconciled to God. Associated historically with Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, and in modern times with writers such as David Bentley Hart and Robin Parry; a persistent but minority stream.

Historicist/this-worldly reading of Gehenna: in Jesus' usage, Gehenna primarily warned of concrete historical judgment on Israel/Jerusalem (e.g., the events of AD 70) rather than a postmortem realm; drawn on by some critical scholars and partially by N.T. Wright, and by full preterists.
basis: Jeremiah 7:30-34 and 19:1-13 (Valley of Hinnom as site of judgment)
Matthew 23:33-38 in context of judgment on Jerusalem

alternatives.meaning: Lexical distinction view (widely held in scholarship rather than a rival theology): 'hell' in older English Bibles conflates distinct terms—Sheol/Hades (the grave or intermediate realm of the dead), Gehenna (final punishment), and Tartarus (2 Peter 2:4)—so Hades/Sheol should not be equated with the hell of final judgment.
basis: Revelation 20:13-14 (Hades itself thrown into the lake of fire)

alternatives.meaning: Hell as purely mythological or psychological symbol: in liberal/demythologizing theology (e.g., influenced by Bultmann or Tillich), hell symbolizes present estrangement, despair, or the existential consequence of alienation from God rather than any postmortem state.
basis: Read as reinterpretation of the Gehenna sayings and Revelation's apocalyptic imagery generally, rather than from specific proof texts

notes: There is broad, recognizable consensus on the core referent: hell denotes final divine judgment and exclusion from God for the unrepentant, symbolized by fire (Gehenna imagery). What remains genuinely contested is the nature and duration of that state—eternal conscious torment (historically dominant), annihilation (growing minority), and universal restoration (persistent minority)—as well as whether the fire imagery is literal or metaphorical. Modern biblical scholarship also uniformly distinguishes Sheol/Hades (realm of the dead) from Gehenna (final punishment), a distinction blurred by the single English word 'hell' in the KJV tradition.
